messages.subject: Cross-overs
messages.body_plain:
In the world of R, I'm having trouble knowing how to handle cross-
overs or mismatches between percentage of application of the dependent
variable and the coefficients glm() gives for each level in a
variable. They usually lined up, but the occasional mismatch makes me
(having been trained with the software GoldVarb) want to resolve the
cross-overs. So, my first question is: Do I need to resolve those
cross-overs or am I worrying myself too much with the percentages and
not enough with the coefficients?

I've noticed that running pairwise interactions mitigates and can even
completely resolve such cross-overs, but I'm unsure about how to
explain in my papers why exactly these interacted variables are
included. Is there something more than the fact that these cross-overs
are resolved and better R-squared and AIC values are obtained with
lrm() and glm() when the pairwise interactions are included?

To take an example, while studying final /s/ aspiration in Spanish,
the interaction between lexical frequency and the following segment
was selected as significant. However, only the interaction between
frequency and coronal consonants, and not other sounds, was selected.
So, is it correct to say that: "Lexical frequency exerts a significant
influence on the realization of final /s/ only when this sound is
followed by a coronal consonant."

Thanks for your help. I can feel the statistical power of R, but I
just don't know how best to explain it.

messages.subject: Re: Cross-overs
messages.body_plain:
Yeah, I wasn't sure if it came out clearly. Here's an example. Final /
s/ in some of my Spanish data reduces:
17% before /p, k/
27% before /t/
58% before other consonants

The factor weights that GoldVarb gives are:
0.40 for /p, k/
0.51 for /t/
0.84 for other consonants

So, the same hierarchy is created regardless of whether you use the
percentages or the factor weights: /p, k/ > /t/ > others. But,
sometimes, because of interaction between independent factor groups,
GoldVarb can give factor weights that do NOT line up with the
percentages (not in the above example, but with other data). When this
happens, I was trained to try to recombine the variants in such a way
that the "cross-over", or mismatch, is resolved and the hierarchy
created by the percentages and the hierarchy created by the factor
weights are the same.

My question is: Is there any reason to try to achieve this sameness of
variant hierarchy between percentages and the coefficients, called
"Estimate" in summary(glm()), given by R in a binary logistic
regression with glm() or lrm()? Maybe the real question is: Is there
any need to worry about the percentages, or should I only worry about
and report the coefficients? Thanks.

messages.subject: Change of website
messages.body_plain:
Given Google's already pathetic support of the Pages and Files
features of Google groups over the last year or so, it's not really a
big surprise that they are now going to discontinue that 'service' as
of 1 November 2010. For now, the Discussion feature should remain
available, and as before you can find a mirror of this group's page
with all the files at <http://www.linguistics.ucsb.edu/faculty/stgries/
research/sflwr/sflwr.html>

Sorry for that, I had trusted Google more than was appropriate, it
seems ...

STG
